passage: When you push a heavy box across the floor, it does not slide forever. It slows down and stops because of friction. Friction is a force that acts between two surfaces that touch each other, and it always acts against the direction of motion. Even surfaces that look smooth have tiny bumps and hollows. When two surfaces press together, these bumps lock into each other, and this interlocking resists sliding. A rough surface such as a brick floor has larger bumps, so it produces more friction than a polished marble floor. The harder the two surfaces are pressed together, the greater the friction. That is why a box full of books is harder to push than an empty one. Friction is not always a nuisance. Without it we could not walk, because our shoes would slip on the ground, and a car could not stop when the driver presses the brakes. Friction also produces heat. If you rub your palms together quickly, they become warm. Sometimes we want to reduce friction. Oil and grease are put between the moving parts of machines, and ball bearings are fitted in the wheels of cycles, because rolling causes much less friction than sliding. On the other hand, the treads on tyres and the grooves on the soles of sports shoes are designed to increase friction and give a better grip.

passage: A simple electric circuit needs three things: a source of electricity such as a cell, a device that uses electricity such as a bulb, and connecting wires that make a complete path. Current flows only when the path is closed. A switch is used to open or close this path. When the switch is on, the circuit is closed and the bulb glows. When it is off, there is a gap in the path and the current stops. A cell has two terminals, a positive terminal and a negative terminal. In a circuit diagram, the longer line stands for the positive terminal. When two or more cells are joined, the positive terminal of one cell must be connected to the negative terminal of the next. This arrangement is called a battery. Bulbs can also be joined one after another in a single path. This is called a series connection. In a series circuit the same current passes through every bulb, and the current is not used up on the way: just as much current returns to the cell as leaves it. However, if one bulb in a series circuit fuses, the path is broken and all the other bulbs go off too. In our homes, lights and fans are not joined in series. They are joined in parallel, so that each one can be switched on or off without affecting the others.

passage: Sound is produced when an object vibrates. A vibration is a rapid to-and-fro motion. When you pluck the string of a sitar, the string vibrates and you hear a sound. When the vibration stops, the sound also stops. In human beings, sound is produced by the voice box, called the larynx, at the upper end of the windpipe. Two vocal cords are stretched across it, and air from the lungs makes them vibrate. Sound needs a medium to travel. It can travel through solids, liquids and gases, but it cannot travel through a vacuum. This is why astronauts on the Moon, where there is no air, talk to each other by radio. Sound travels faster in solids than in air. If you put your ear to one end of a long table and a friend taps the other end gently, you hear the tap clearly through the wood. The number of vibrations in one second is called the frequency, and it is measured in hertz. A high frequency gives a high-pitched sound, like a whistle, while a low frequency gives a low-pitched sound, like a drum. The human ear can hear sounds with frequencies from about 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz. Sounds below this range are called infrasonic, and sounds above it are called ultrasonic. Bats and dolphins can hear ultrasonic sounds.

passage: When light falls on a smooth, shiny surface such as a mirror, it bounces back. This is called reflection. The ray of light that falls on the mirror is called the incident ray, and the ray that bounces back is called the reflected ray. Imagine a line drawn at the point where the light hits the mirror, standing straight up from the surface at 90 degrees. This line is called the normal. The angle between the incident ray and the normal is the angle of incidence, and the angle between the reflected ray and the normal is the angle of reflection. The first law of reflection says that these two angles are always equal. So if a ray strikes a mirror at an angle of incidence of 30 degrees, it will be reflected at 30 degrees. The second law says that the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane. A plane mirror forms an image that is upright and of the same size as the object. The image appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. If you stand 2 metres in front of a mirror, your image seems to be 2 metres behind it, that is, 4 metres away from you. The image is also laterally inverted, which means that your left hand appears as the right hand of the image. This is why the word AMBULANCE is written in reverse on the front of ambulances.

passage: Magnets attract objects made of iron, nickel and cobalt. Materials that are attracted by a magnet are called magnetic materials, while materials such as wood, plastic, rubber and glass are non-magnetic. Every magnet has two poles, a north pole and a south pole. The attraction is strongest near the poles. If a bar magnet is hung freely from a thread, it always comes to rest pointing in the north-south direction. This property is used in a compass, which travellers and sailors have used for centuries to find directions. When two magnets are brought close, like poles repel each other and unlike poles attract each other. Breaking a magnet does not separate its poles: each broken piece becomes a new magnet with its own north and south pole. Magnets lose their magnetism if they are heated, hammered or dropped often. To keep them safe, bar magnets are stored in pairs with their unlike poles on the same side, separated by a piece of wood.

passage: Meena watched her grandfather cut vegetables in the kitchen. He sharpened his knife on a stone before he began. 'Why do you do that?' she asked. 'A sharp knife cuts easily,' he said. Meena later learnt the reason in her science class. Pressure is the force acting on a unit area of a surface. When the same force acts on a smaller area, the pressure is greater. The sharp edge of a knife has a very small area, so the force from Grandfather's hand produces a large pressure and the knife cuts through a tomato easily. A blunt knife has a wider edge, so the same force spreads over a larger area and the pressure is less. The same idea explains many things Meena had seen. Porters carrying heavy loads on their heads place a round piece of cloth under the load. The cloth increases the area of contact, so the pressure on the head is reduced and the load is easier to carry. School bags have broad straps for the same reason, while thin straps cut painfully into the shoulders. Nails and pins have pointed tips so that they enter wood with little effort. Liquids and gases also exert pressure. Water presses on the walls of its container, and the pressure increases with depth. That is why the walls of a dam are made much thicker at the bottom than at the top.

passage: Some foods taste sour because they contain acids. Lemon juice contains citric acid, curd contains lactic acid, and vinegar contains acetic acid. Substances that taste bitter and feel soapy, such as baking soda, are called bases. Tasting is not a safe way to test a substance, so we use indicators. An indicator changes its colour when it is added to an acid or a base. Litmus is a natural indicator obtained from lichens. Blue litmus paper turns red in an acid, while red litmus paper turns blue in a base. Turmeric is another natural indicator found in every Indian kitchen. A turmeric stain on a white cloth turns red when soap, which is a base, is rubbed on it, and it turns yellow again when washed with plenty of water. China rose petals give a solution that turns dark pink in an acid and green in a base. When an acid is mixed with a base, they cancel each other's effect. This reaction is called neutralisation, and it produces a salt and water, along with heat. Neutralisation is useful in daily life. An ant bite injects formic acid into the skin, and the pain can be relieved by rubbing on a mild base such as moist baking soda. Farmers add quicklime or slaked lime to soil that is too acidic.

passage: Changes around us can be grouped into two kinds. In a physical change, a substance changes its shape, size or state, but no new substance is formed. When ice melts into water, it is still water. When a sheet of paper is cut into pieces, each piece is still paper. Many physical changes can be reversed: water can be frozen back into ice. In a chemical change, one or more new substances are formed. When a piece of paper burns, it turns into ash, smoke and gases, and you cannot get the paper back. Burning of wood, cooking of food, rusting of iron and the souring of milk into curd are all chemical changes. A chemical change is often shown by signs such as the release of heat or light, a change in colour, the production of a gas, or a change in smell. When baking soda is added to vinegar, bubbles of carbon dioxide gas are produced, which shows that a new substance has formed. Some processes involve both kinds of change. When a candle burns, the wax first melts, which is a physical change. The wax vapour then burns in the flame to produce carbon dioxide, water vapour, heat and light, which is a chemical change. Crystallisation, in which pure crystals of a substance such as copper sulphate are obtained from its solution, is a physical change.

passage: Salt is not mined only from the ground. Along the coasts of Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, a lot of our common salt is obtained from sea water. Sea water is let into shallow pits called salt pans and left there. The heat of the sun slowly turns the water into vapour, a process called evaporation, and the salt is left behind as white crystals. This salt is then collected and purified. Evaporation is one of several methods used to separate the parts of a mixture. If a mixture contains a solid that does not dissolve in a liquid, such as sand in water, the sand can first be allowed to settle at the bottom. This is called sedimentation. The clear water above can then be poured off gently into another vessel without disturbing the sand, which is called decantation. To remove the last fine particles, the water can be passed through filter paper. This is filtration. In villages, husk is separated from grain by winnowing, in which the mixture is dropped from a height in the wind, and the light husk is blown away while the heavier grain falls straight down. Stones are picked out of rice and dal by hand, which is called handpicking. Sieving is used in flour mills and at construction sites to separate fine particles from larger ones.

passage: Elements can be broadly divided into metals and non-metals. Metals such as iron, copper, aluminium and gold are usually hard and shiny. Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity, which is why cooking vessels are made of metal and electric wires are made of copper. Metals also make a ringing sound when struck, so school bells are made of metal. Non-metals such as sulphur, carbon, oxygen and phosphorus behave very differently. Solid non-metals are generally soft and dull, and they break into pieces when hammered. They are poor conductors of heat and electricity. There are a few exceptions. Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature. Graphite, a form of carbon, is a non-metal that conducts electricity, and it is used in the electrodes of cells. Diamond, another form of carbon, is the hardest natural substance known. Metals and non-metals also react differently with oxygen. passage: Combustion is a chemical process in which a substance reacts with oxygen to give off heat. A substance that can burn is called a combustible substance or a fuel. For combustion to happen, three things are needed together: a fuel, air to supply oxygen, and enough heat to raise the fuel to its ignition temperature. The ignition temperature is the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire. Kerosene has a low ignition temperature, so it catches fire easily, while wood must be heated much more. Removing any one of these three things puts a fire out, and this is the idea behind every fire extinguisher. Water is the most common extinguisher. It cools the burning material below its ignition temperature, and the steam it produces also helps to keep air away. But water should never be used on fires involving electrical equipment, because water conducts electricity and can give a shock. Water is also not suitable for oil and petrol fires, because the oil floats on water and keeps burning. For such fires, carbon dioxide is the best extinguisher. Being heavier than air, it forms a blanket around the fire, cutting off the supply of oxygen, and it does not harm electrical equipment. Covering a small fire with a blanket or sand works in the same way.

passage: Digestion is the process of breaking down food into simple substances that the body can absorb. It begins in the mouth. Our teeth break food into small pieces, and saliva from the salivary glands begins to change starch into sugar. The tongue mixes the food with saliva and pushes it down into the food pipe, or oesophagus. The walls of the food pipe contract and relax in waves, moving the food down to the stomach. The stomach is a thick-walled bag. Its inner lining releases hydrochloric acid and digestive juices. The acid kills many bacteria that enter with the food, and the juices begin to break down proteins. From the stomach, the partly digested food passes into the small intestine, which is about 7.5 metres long and is tightly coiled. Here the food is completely digested with the help of bile from the liver and juice from the pancreas. The inner wall of the small intestine has thousands of finger-like outgrowths called villi. They greatly increase the surface area for absorption, and the digested food passes through them into the blood vessels. The blood then carries the food to every part of the body. Undigested food moves into the large intestine, which is shorter but wider, where water and some salts are absorbed. The remaining waste is removed from the body through the anus.

passage: Many people use the words breathing and respiration as if they mean the same thing, but they are different processes. Breathing is the movement of air into and out of the lungs. When we breathe in, the chest cavity expands and air rushes into the lungs. When we breathe out, the chest cavity becomes smaller and air is pushed out. Respiration is what happens inside the cells of the body. In respiration, glucose from our food is broken down to release energy, which the cells use for every activity, from moving a muscle to thinking. When oxygen is used, the glucose is broken down completely into carbon dioxide and water, and this is called aerobic respiration. When there is not enough oxygen, glucose is broken down only partly. This is anaerobic respiration. During hard exercise, our leg muscles may respire anaerobically and produce lactic acid, which causes cramps. Yeast also respires without oxygen and produces alcohol, which is why it is used in making bread and in brewing. Plants respire too, all the time, day and night, through tiny pores in their leaves and through their roots. It is a common mistake to think that plants respire only at night. During the day their respiration is simply hidden, because photosynthesis uses up more carbon dioxide than respiration releases.

passage: Most green plants make their own food, but a few plants also trap insects. The pitcher plant is one of them. It is found in the hills of Meghalaya and in some other parts of north-eastern India. Part of its leaf is shaped like a jug, or pitcher, and the tip of the leaf forms a lid over its mouth. The rim of the pitcher is slippery and often brightly coloured, and it produces a sweet substance that attracts insects. When an insect lands on the rim, it slips and falls inside. Hair inside the pitcher points downwards, so the insect cannot climb back out. At the bottom, the insect drowns in a liquid that contains digestive juices, and its body is slowly broken down and absorbed by the plant. Why should a green plant that can make its own food catch insects at all? The answer lies in the soil. Pitcher plants usually grow in soil that is poor in nitrogen, a nutrient that all plants need to make proteins. The insects supply the nitrogen that the soil lacks. So the pitcher plant still carries out photosynthesis in its green leaves; the insects are not its main source of food but a supplement. Other insect-eating plants include the Venus flytrap and the sundew.

passage: The heart is a muscular organ about the size of your fist. It lies in the chest, slightly towards the left, and it pumps blood to all parts of the body without stopping, all through our lives. The human heart has four chambers. The two upper chambers are called atria and the two lower chambers are called ventricles. The right side of the heart receives blood that has given its oxygen to the body and sends it to the lungs. In the lungs the blood picks up fresh oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide. This oxygen-rich blood returns to the left side of the heart, which pumps it to the rest of the body. The wall between the left and right sides keeps the two kinds of blood from mixing. Valves between the chambers allow blood to flow in only one direction. Blood leaves the heart through arteries, which have thick, elastic walls because the blood in them is under high pressure. Blood returns to the heart through veins, which have thinner walls and contain valves of their own. Each contraction of the heart is a heartbeat, and the push of blood in the arteries can be felt as the pulse at the wrist. A healthy adult at rest has a pulse rate of about 72 beats per minute, while for a small child it is higher. During exercise, the heart beats faster to supply more oxygen to the muscles.

passage: Microorganisms are living things so small that they can be seen only through a microscope. They include bacteria, fungi, protozoa and some algae. Although some cause diseases, many microorganisms are very useful to us. When a little curd is added to warm milk and left for a few hours, the milk sets into curd. This happens because a bacterium called Lactobacillus multiplies in the milk and converts it into curd. The same kind of bacteria helps in making cheese and pickles. Yeast, a fungus, is used in making bread, idli and dosa batter. As yeast respires, it releases carbon dioxide gas, and the bubbles of gas make the dough rise and the batter soft and spongy. Microorganisms are also used to make medicines. In 1929 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould growing on one of his plates had stopped the growth of bacteria around it. From this mould the first antibiotic, penicillin, was made. Antibiotics kill or stop the growth of disease-causing bacteria, but they do not work against viruses, such as those that cause the common cold. In the soil, some bacteria and blue-green algae fix nitrogen from the air and make the soil more fertile. Other microorganisms break down dead plants and animals into simple substances, which keeps the environment clean.

passage: Flowers are the reproductive parts of a plant. The male part of a flower is the stamen, which produces pollen grains. The female part is the pistil, which contains the ovules in its lower part, the ovary. For seeds to form, pollen must reach the sticky top of the pistil, called the stigma. The transfer of pollen from the stamen to the stigma is called pollination. If the pollen lands on the stigma of the same flower, it is called self-pollination. If it is carried to a flower on another plant of the same kind, it is called cross-pollination. Plants cannot move, so they depend on carriers. Wind carries the light, dry pollen of maize and grasses over long distances. Insects such as bees and butterflies visit brightly coloured, sweet-smelling flowers to drink nectar. As they move from flower to flower, pollen sticks to their bodies and is carried along. After pollination, the pollen grain grows a tube down to the ovule, and the male cell joins the egg cell. This joining is called fertilisation. The fertilised egg develops into an embryo, the ovule becomes a seed, and the ovary grows into a fruit. Seeds are then scattered away from the parent plant, by wind, water and animals, so that the new plants do not compete with each other for light and water.

passage: A plant must move water from its roots to leaves that may be many metres above the ground, and it does this without a pump. The water travels through a tissue called xylem. Xylem is made up of long tubes formed from cells joined end to end. Surprisingly, the main cells of the xylem are dead when they do their job. As they mature, they lose their living contents, and the cross walls between them break down, leaving hollow, continuous pipes. Their thick walls, strengthened by a substance called lignin, keep the pipes from collapsing and also help the stem to stand upright. Water enters the roots from the soil and is pulled up through these tubes. The main force that pulls it is transpiration, the loss of water vapour through tiny pores called stomata on the leaves. As water evaporates from the leaves, it creates a pull that draws more water up the xylem, like drinking through a straw. A second tissue, the phloem, carries food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant, such as the roots and fruits. Unlike xylem, the main cells of phloem are living. Together, xylem and phloem form the vascular bundles that can be seen as veins in a leaf. A large tree may lose hundreds of litres of water on a hot day through transpiration.

passage: In the eighteenth century, smallpox was one of the most feared diseases in the world. It killed millions of people and left many survivors with deep scars. An English doctor named Edward Jenner noticed something interesting in the countryside. Milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease from cows, did not seem to get smallpox. In 1796 Jenner tested this idea. He took material from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid and put it into a small cut on the arm of a boy named James Phipps. The boy became slightly ill and then recovered. Some weeks later, Jenner exposed him to smallpox, and the boy did not fall sick. Jenner called this method vaccination, from vacca, the Latin word for cow. Today we know how it works. A vaccine contains dead or weakened germs, or parts of them. When it enters the body, the body produces antibodies to fight these germs, and it remembers how to make them. If the real germs attack later, the body can destroy them quickly, before they cause disease. Vaccines have since been made against many diseases, including polio, measles and tetanus. After a worldwide vaccination campaign, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980. India was declared free of polio in 2014, after years of pulse polio drives in which every child under five was given drops.

passage: Ashoka was one of the most famous rulers of ancient India. He belonged to the Mauryan dynasty, which was founded by his grandfather, Chandragupta Maurya, with the help of a wise minister named Chanakya. Ashoka became king in about 268 BCE and ruled a vast empire with its capital at Pataliputra, near present-day Patna. About eight years after he became king, Ashoka fought a war to conquer Kalinga, in present-day Odisha. The war was terrible. Thousands of people were killed and many more were taken captive. Ashoka was so filled with sorrow at the suffering he saw that he decided never to fight a war of conquest again. He turned to the teachings of the Buddha and began to follow what he called dhamma. Ashoka's dhamma was not a new religion. It asked people to be kind to animals, to respect their elders and teachers, to treat servants and slaves well, and to respect the religions of others. To spread these ideas, Ashoka had his messages carved on rocks and on polished stone pillars across his empire. Most of these inscriptions were written in the Prakrit language using the Brahmi script. The lions on top of his pillar at Sarnath form the national emblem of India today, and the wheel on it appears on our national flag.

passage: The Mughal emperors ruled a very large and varied empire, and they needed a system to manage it. Akbar, who ruled from 1556 to 1605, organised the administration with great care. He introduced the mansabdari system. A mansabdar was a person who held a mansab, meaning a rank or position in the emperor's service. Instead, they were given revenue assignments called jagirs, which allowed them to collect taxes from certain areas. Under Akbar, mansabdars did not live in their jagirs, and the emperor's officers made sure that the taxes collected were fair. To fix the land revenue, Akbar's revenue minister, Todar Mal, carried out a careful survey of crop yields, prices and the area cultivated over ten years. The tax was then fixed for each crop in cash. The empire was divided into provinces called subas, each governed by a subadar. passage: The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word mausim, which means season. India's climate is called a monsoon climate because the direction of the winds reverses with the seasons. In summer, the land heats up much faster than the sea. By May, an area of low pressure forms over the plains of north-western India. The air over the Indian Ocean is cooler, so the pressure there is higher. Winds blow from high pressure to low pressure, so moist winds from the ocean begin to move towards the land. These are the south-west monsoon winds. They pick up a great deal of moisture as they cross the warm ocean. The monsoon usually reaches the southern tip of Kerala by the first week of June and spreads over almost the whole country by mid-July. When the moist winds are forced to rise over the Western Ghats, they cool and drop heavy rain on the western slopes. The eastern side receives much less rain because it lies in the rain shadow. Mawsynram in Meghalaya receives one of the highest rainfalls in the world. By October, the land cools and the winds reverse, blowing from the land towards the sea. These are the retreating monsoon winds, which bring rain to the Coromandel coast of Tamil Nadu in October and November.

passage: Soil is a very important resource, because almost all our food grows in it. Soil is formed when rocks are slowly broken down by changes in temperature, running water, wind and living things, over thousands of years. India has many types of soil. Alluvial soil is the most widespread. It is deposited by rivers such as the Ganga, the Brahmaputra and the Indus, and it covers the northern plains. It is very fertile and is good for growing rice, wheat and sugarcane. Black soil, also called regur soil, is found in the Deccan plateau, in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh. It is formed from volcanic rocks and is excellent for growing cotton. Black soil holds moisture well and develops deep cracks in hot weather. Red and yellow soils develop on old crystalline rocks in the eastern and southern parts of the Deccan. They get their red colour from iron. Laterite soil forms in areas with high temperature and heavy rainfall, where the rain washes away many nutrients. With proper manure, it is used to grow tea, coffee and cashew. Arid soils, found in Rajasthan, are sandy and salty. Soil erosion, the removal of the top layer of soil by wind and water, is a serious problem. Planting trees, terrace farming on slopes and contour ploughing help to prevent it.

Many of the species living there are endemic, which means they are found nowhere else on Earth. passage: When we dig a well, we usually find water at some depth below the ground. This water is called groundwater. Many people imagine that groundwater flows in underground rivers or lies in large lakes beneath the surface, but this is mostly not true. Groundwater fills the tiny spaces between grains of sand and soil, and the cracks in rocks, much like water fills a sponge. When it rains, some of the water soaks into the ground. This process is called infiltration. The water moves down until it reaches a layer of rock that it cannot pass through. Above this layer, the spaces between the particles become completely filled with water. The upper level of this water-filled layer is called the water table. A layer of rock or soil that stores water and allows it to flow through is called an aquifer. The water table is not fixed. It rises after good rains and falls when more water is drawn out than is put back. In many parts of India, water is pumped out by tube wells for irrigation faster than rain can refill the ground, and the water table has dropped by many metres. Paving every surface with concrete also reduces infiltration. Rainwater harvesting, in which rainwater from rooftops is led into pits or old wells, helps to recharge groundwater.

passage: The Earth moves in two ways. It spins on its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, and one full spin takes about 24 hours. This movement is called rotation, and it causes day and night. At any moment, the half of the Earth facing the Sun has day, while the other half has night. The Earth also travels around the Sun in a path called its orbit. One full trip takes about 365 days and 6 hours, which is one year. This movement is called revolution. Every four years the extra hours add up to one whole day, so February then has 29 days, and that year is called a leap year. The Earth's axis is not upright. passage: India is a secular country. In the Indian Constitution, secularism means that the State does not favour any one religion, and that every person is free to follow, practise and spread the religion of their choice. The State does not have an official religion. However, Indian secularism is different from the idea of a complete wall between the State and religion that some other countries follow. In India, the State keeps what is called a principled distance from religion. This means that it usually stays away from religious matters, but it can step in when a religious practice goes against the rights guaranteed by the Constitution. For example, the Constitution abolished untouchability, even though some people defended it as part of their religious tradition. The State can also make exceptions out of respect for religious practices. The law requires people riding two-wheelers to wear helmets, but Sikhs who wear turbans are allowed not to wear a helmet. The aim of all this is to make sure that no religious group dominates another, that members of the same religion do not dominate each other, and that the State does not force any religion on people. In government schools, therefore, the celebration of a religious festival as an official school event is not allowed, but students are free to celebrate festivals at home.

passage: The Constitution of India gives every citizen certain basic rights, called Fundamental Rights. They protect people against the misuse of power by the government and by other people. passage: Poor households in villages often find it hard to get loans from banks. Banks ask for collateral, such as land or a building, that can be sold if the loan is not repaid, and many poor people have nothing to offer. They are forced to borrow from moneylenders, who may charge interest as high as five per cent a month. Self Help Groups, or SHGs, were formed to solve this problem. A typical SHG has 15 to 20 members, usually women from the same village. Each member saves a small amount every month, perhaps fifty or a hundred rupees. Over time, the savings become a useful fund. Members can take small loans from the group to meet their needs, and the group decides the purpose, the amount and the repayment schedule. The interest charged is far lower than that of a moneylender. After a year or two of regular saving and repayment, the group becomes eligible for a loan from a bank. The bank lends to the group as a whole, without collateral, because the members are responsible for repaying together. With such loans, women have started small businesses such as tailoring, poultry and making pickles. SHGs also give women a chance to meet regularly and discuss issues such as health, education and domestic violence. passage: Every day, every household throws away some waste. Vegetable peels, leftover food, paper, plastic bags, bottles and broken toys all end up in the dustbin. passage: The Sun is the main source of energy for the Earth, and solar energy can be turned directly into electricity using solar panels. A solar panel is made of many solar cells, usually made of silicon. When sunlight falls on a solar cell, it produces a small electric current. A single cell gives only about half a volt, so many cells are joined together in a panel. India receives plenty of sunshine, with about 300 sunny days a year in most parts of the country. A rooftop solar system of 1 kilowatt needs about 10 square metres of roof space and can produce about 4 units of electricity on a sunny day, which is enough to run a few lights, fans and a television in a small home. Solar energy does not produce smoke or harmful gases, and the sunlight itself costs nothing. However, solar panels produce no electricity at night and less on cloudy days, so the extra electricity produced during the day is stored in batteries or sent to the main electricity grid. The cost of solar panels has fallen sharply over the last fifteen years. The village of Dharnai in Bihar became one of the first in India to run entirely on a solar micro-grid in 2014. The Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan, spread over about 56 square kilometres, is one of the largest solar parks in the world.
